title: TB5-05258
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): She appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated April 29, 2015, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of the People's Republic of China. She appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated April 29, 2015, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.
The Appellant did not submit documents for consideration as new evidence pursuant to s.110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA or the Act).

The Appellant's claim was heard with that of her parents and her brother, requiring three sittings. This appeal is only for the Appellant who is a XXXX year old minor girl. Her parents and her brother are seeking judicial review of the RPD's decision. The Appellant's father was her Designated Representative at the RPD hearing as confirmed by the RAD
In rejecting the claims, the RPD found that the Appellants are not credible.
The RAD confirms the RPD's determination pursuant to s. 111(1)(a) of the Act. The Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. Background

The Appellant is afraid to return to China due to the actions of her parents who "violated the family planning policy"1 of the People's Republic of China. The claim of the Appellant is based on her membership in particular social group and she fears a denial of social services should she return to China.

The Appellant's parents (XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX) are citizens of China and her brother, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was born in Hong Kong in XXXX and thus a permanent resident of Hong Kong. These three arrived in Canada in XXXX 2012. The Appellant alleged before the RPD that she stayed back in China and lived with her grandmother and was a student at middle school. Her grandmother received a notice from the school that the Appellant is suspended due to her parents' family planning problems. The appellant further alleged before the RPD2 that her grandmother was told that the Appellant was not allowed to attend the school until her parents submit themselves to the family planning officers. The Appellant left China with the help of an agent on XXXX 2014 and arrived in Canada via the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Her claim was joined with that of her other family members as per the RPD rules. Appellant's issues

The Appellant's issues are: Did the Board err by a) Failing to make a proper determination regarding the minor Appellant by erring in relation to the decision as a whole which naturally would impact the decision of the minor Appellant. b) Failing to properly consider and assess the testimony of the adult female Appellant and thereby finding that the Mainland travel permit is sufficient evidence that authorities were aware that they had a second child. c) Failing to properly assess the sur place aspect of the claim. d) Failing to consider whatsoever a major ground for the Appellant's claim.
I will rephrase the issue as follows: is the Appellant a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection? Standard of review / Role of the RAD
The Appellant did not make submissions regarding the role of the RAD or the standard of review the RAD should apply.

The jurisprudence on the role of the RAD is evolving, however, at present; guidance provided by Justice Phelan in Huruglica3 seems to be generally accepted. I am guided by this case where the court stated the following: [54] Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision. [55] In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is a "palpable and overriding error."

Moreover in Tkachuk4 the Federal court stated, "I have considered the high degree of deference owed to the Board with respect to credibility, given that the Board observes the applicant and can probe an applicant's testimony and the manner in which it is provided".

Guided by the federal court, I will consider the evidence in totality and arrive at my own determination. Also guided by Huruglica, I will recognize and respect the RPD's credibility findings where it had particular advantage. Merits of the claim

The claim of the Appellant is a derivative claim-arising out of the alleged actions of her parents and she is afraid that she will be denied social benefits including education should she return to China.
In support of this allegation, the appellant provided only one document, a brief notice from the school5 dated XXXX XXXX, 2013.

The RPD had considered this notice and decided to place no weight on it for the following reasons. The Appellant's parents had testified at the RPD that the Chinese authorities became aware of their second child, XXXX, only in XXXX 2012 even though he was born in XXXX in Hong Kong and came to China XXXX days after his birth, with proper documents. The RPD found that the authorities became aware of their second child in XXXX and not in 2012 as the Appellant's parents alleged. The school notice is dated XXXX 2013, almost a year and a half after the parents allege the Chinese authorities became aware of second child's existence.

The RPD had two concerns regarding this notice; first, the timing of the letter (a year and half delay after the parents are found to have violated the one child policy) and second, lack of documentary evidence to support the allegation that the Chinese authorities take such actions. One child policy in China is a policy of national importance and the National Documentation Package (NDP) of China contains huge volumes of information regarding this policy and how it is administered, therefore it would reasonably be expected that there was some documentary evidence to support that the school will send such a notice.

In addition to documents in the NDP, the Appellant also provided large volumes of documents (e.g; exhibit 11 of the RPD's Record, pages 288 to 553) that confirm the NDP package information that the children born out of one child policy may not be registered and may not have any legal existence and therefore may have difficulty going to school.6 This document further shows7 that "Officials also may refuse to issue residence cards to "out of plan" children, thereby denying them education and other state benefits."

The Appellant in this case was born in XXXX, she is registered, there is no evidence that she can be de-registered or that her registration has been revoked. Moreover there is no evidence to support that a child who was already attending school will be given notice that she cannot continue her education in the middle school. The Appellants were given opportunity to explain these concerns of the RPD, but there is no reasonable explanation, and therefore I find that the RPD did not err in placing little weight on this document. In addition to finding the RPD's concerns supportable, I also note that the letter states, "He'll be in the suspended from school until his parents complete the procedures required by the birth control office." I find it strange that such an allegedly important document issued by the school would make an error about the gender of the appellant. Moreover, the Appellant is the first born child, and the sanctions are placed on the second child, not the first child.

The alleged notice from the school is the only documentary evidence to support the Appellant's claim. The Appellant's parents allege that their second child was discovered in 2012, the RPD found that incredible and found that the Hong Kong born child was issued proper travel documents in XXXX, XXXX days after his birth.

The RPD found that the Appellant's parents are not credible due to several concerns. The RPD found that the Appellant's testimony regarding their second child was not credible on the issue of whether the Chinese authorities were aware that the minor, a citizen of Hong Kong, is their second child. The RPD found that the Chinese authorities were aware of the fact but the Appellants submit that the RPD erred in this finding and argues that the RPD "ignored relevant testimony from the female Appellant regarding obtaining a Chinese travel document for the child" who was born in Hong Kong. The Appellant submitted in paragraph 16 of the memorandum8 at page 60 of exhibit P-2: It is submitted that the Board failed to consider the adult female Appellant's testimony that the MTP was not issued by the Family Planning Office and that as far as the Appellant is aware, the document is a genuine document but that rather it had been obtained by the smuggler and not her, thereby suggesting that the document could be genuine notwithstanding that it was improperly obtained.

The Appellant does not state how or where the RPD ignored the testimony of the Appellant. A review of the record shows that the RPD weighed evidence and noted that the travel document was issued by the authorities XXXX days after the child's birth, and that the Appellant provided conflicting information about the authenticity of the travel card (travel document) and how often it was used. The RPD cited detailed objective documentary evidence in its reasons at paragraph 15. I find that the RPD's finding is supportable as I would come to the same finding.

The Appellant's parents also provided conflicting testimony regarding the authenticity of the travel card for their child XXXX, who was born in Hong Kong in XXXX. They initially stated it was a real card, and this is why it was returned to them after it was used for the minor claimant to enter China. In addition, they provided inconsistent testimony about how often the travel card was used. I find that the RPD's finding is supportable as I would also arrive at this finding.

The Appellant's parents testified before the RPD that her father lost his job in XXXX 2012 after the authorities became aware that they have a second child born in XXXX, and provided a copy of a brief letter of dismissal in support of their allegation. The RPD noted that the Appellant provided conflicting information about the alleged letter of dismissal;9 how and why it was received by them.

The RPD had several other concerns about the authenticity of this notice as well that were not explained reasonably. The RPD noted in its reasons several unexplained or unreasonably explained inconsistencies about the circumstances and confusion under which they received this letter. I also note that the title of the Appellant's father in this letter is written as "XXXX" at the XXXX which contradicts his other documents which state that he was a XXXX.

The Appellants provided an alleged Notice from the "Birth Control Office" stating that they were "raising a child outside the state plan," and it is dated XXXX XXXX, 2012. This notice that a financial penalty of "a social upbringing payment of 150,000 must be collected." The Federal court in Li Xing Chen stated [26] The findings of the Board with respect to this issue were open to it on the face of the record before it. Moreover, there is a long line of jurisprudence to the effect that the fine or "social compensation fee" charged to families that have more than one child is not persecution within the meaning of the Convention; Huang, paras 23-26; Wang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 636 (CanLII), para 27.

The case of Chen and this case have many similarities that include the province of residence and issue of second child. In both cases, the persons lived in the province of Guangdong. In both cases alleged fears are similar-forced sterilization or IUD insertion and or financial penalty. In Chen the court noted in paragraph 23: Although the applicant says that she and her husband still fear a risk of forced sterilization, that risk, is speculative. The Board noted that there are local significant variances with respect to degree and nature of enforcement of Family Planning policies and the Board declined to infer, based on the evidence, that forced sterilization remained a serious possibility.

In this case the RPD came to a similar and supportable finding on the issue of financial penalty. The Appellant submits that financial penalty is high and persecutory. It is noted that the Appellants are well-off and have travelled extensively internationally, managed to have a child in Hong Kong and another child in Canada. The RPD noted these and noted re-availment as an issue for the Appellant's family and thus for the Appellant.
The Appellant submits that the sur place nature of the claim was ignored. I am not persuaded. The RPD considered it and I am not persuaded that it has a direct bearing on this Appellant.

The RPD is owed deference in its credibility findings and after a careful consideration of the RPD's determination and a review of the totality of the evidence before me; I find that the Appellant's allegations are not supportable by credible evidence.

The Appellant lived with her grandmother and there is no reason for me to believe that she will not be able to return to China and live with her grandmother and continue her studies if that is what she desires.
Based on the foregoing I find that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

This appeal is dismissed.
